questions.q: A reporter has a strong subject, decades of political violence, but readers drift away after the opening. What would Keefe's approach in Say Nothing suggest?
choices: Open with a timeline so readers can orient themselves
Build the book around one question readers want answered, like a disappearance, and let the history follow it
Cut the history and write only the crime
Put the thesis in the first paragraph, inverted-pyramid style
questions.explain: In Say Nothing, Jean McConville's disappearance is the engine that carries readers through the history of the Troubles.

questions.q: Keefe holds back his most explosive finding until the final chapters of Say Nothing. What keeps this honest in nonfiction?
choices: He invents a red herring to mislead the reader first
He never tells the reader there is a question
He delays the answer until the story has earned it, without distorting what's true
He presents it as fiction
questions.explain: Withholding in nonfiction means delay, not distortion: the reader knows the question exists.

questions.q: Why does Say Nothing follow Dolours Price, Brendan Hughes, Gerry Adams and the McConville children rather than one hero?
choices: Each sees the same events from a different side, so a few closely followed lives carry the whole history
Because the hero's journey requires a mentor and a threshold guardian
To fit the three-act structure
Because none of them could be interviewed
questions.explain: Multiple protagonists across decades let a lean structure cover a long, contested history.

questions.q: What made the Boston College Belfast Project so valuable, and so fraught, as a source?
choices: It was a government report released under freedom of information
It contained recordings of former paramilitaries made on a promise of secrecy until their deaths, which later broke down in court
It was a set of novels based on the Troubles
It was Keefe's own interview archive
questions.explain: Oral histories made in confidence are candid, but the legal fight over the tapes broke the promise of secrecy.

questions.q: A powerful family declines to be interviewed for your book. What would Keefe do?
choices: Drop the subject
Write their thoughts as if you'd interviewed them
Use only anonymous sources and skip attribution
Write around them: build them from documents, others' memories and their public words, attributing each claim and printing denials
questions.explain: Keefe says he enjoys the challenge of writearounds; the Sacklers didn't cooperate with Empire of Pain.

questions.q: The podcast Wind of Change ends without proving or disproving its rumor. What does this show about a mystery structure?
choices: It promises an investigation, not necessarily a solution, and should be honest about that
Every mystery must end with a confession
A podcast should never use a mystery
The rumor should have been presented as true
questions.explain: A mystery-driven story owes the reader an honest account of what was and wasn't found.

questions.q: How do Keefe's magazine pieces typically open?
choices: With a statement of the issue and statistics
With the author explaining why he took the assignment
With a person in a specific moment, before the larger subject arrives
With a list of key questions
questions.explain: Like the feature formula, he starts with a scene and a person, then widens to why it matters.

ideas: Build a work of history around a single disappearance, so the reader's need to know who did it carries them through decades of politics.
Some journalists hate writing about people who won't cooperate, but treat it as a challenge: build them from records, others' memories and their own public words.
Use an oral history recorded on a promise of secrecy until death to write the inner lives of people who died before you began.
Hold back your own most explosive finding until the final chapters, after the reader has lived with everyone involved.
